name: Clos des Papes Châteauneuf-du-Pape 2011
text:
## Clos des Papes Châteauneuf-du-Pape 2011

**The story.** [Clos des Papes](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Clos+des+Papes,+Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k) is one of the great old names of [Châteauneuf-du-Pape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC), and for many people its single best wine. The name is literal: one of the family's parcels lies near the ruined [papal castle](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Ch%C3%A2teau+des+Papes,+Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k) and was once enclosed by walls, a "clos" ([Skurnik](https://www.skurnik.com/producer/clos-des-papes-2/)). The Avril family has lived in the village for centuries. Records from the second half of the 1700s show Avrils serving as the village's treasurers and municipal consuls ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/clos-des-papes-chateauneuf-du-pape-wine)).

The first Paul Avril, born in 1873, who spent "91 great years" in the appellation, began selling wine under the Clos des Papes label in 1896, making it one of the first estates in the whole [Rhône Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rh%C3%B4ne_wine) to bottle and sell its own wine. He was also one of the people behind the creation of the appellation itself. A second Paul Avril joined in 1963 and died in 2009. Today the estate is run by Paul-Vincent Avril, born in 1965, who joined in 1988 ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/clos-des-papes-chateauneuf-du-pape-wine)). He studied wine in [Burgundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgundy_wine) in the 1980s and worked abroad first, including a spell with Dr John Middleton at Mount Mary in Australia's [Yarra Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yarra_Valley) ([Skurnik](https://www.skurnik.com/producer/clos-des-papes-2/)) and one at [Château Mouton Rothschild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_Mouton_Rothschild) in Bordeaux ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/clos-des-papes-chateauneuf-du-pape-wine)).

**One red, no special cuvées.** Unusually for a top Châteauneuf estate, Clos des Papes makes just one red and one white, with no prestige bottling. Paul-Vincent believes a special cuvée would only take the best grapes away from the wine the family has made for more than a century ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/clos-des-papes-chateauneuf-du-pape-wine)). That is why critics treat the "plain" Clos des Papes as a benchmark for the whole appellation.

**The vineyards.** About 35 hectares, spread over some 24 separate parcels across the appellation ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/clos-des-papes-chateauneuf-du-pape-wine); Skurnik counts 30 parcels and 40 hectares). They range from the big rounded stones of [La Crau](https://www.google.com/maps?q=La+Crau,+Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k) to sand, limestone and gravel. Some of the best [Grenache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenache) grows on sandy soils in the west and south-east of the appellation, while the north-east parcels sit on stones, clay and limestone, including vines near [Courthézon](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Courth%C3%A9zon,+Vaucluse,+France&t=k). Blending all these soils is part of what gives the wine its complexity. The vines average 50 years or more, and yields are tiny: often under 21 hectolitres per hectare for the old vines, roughly half or a third of what the rules allow ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/clos-des-papes-chateauneuf-du-pape-wine); [Skurnik](https://www.skurnik.com/producer/clos-des-papes-2/)). The estate was certified [organic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_farming) in 2010.

**How it's made.** The grapes are picked by hand and, since 1991, fully destemmed. The varieties are fermented together with their own wild yeasts, parcel by parcel, then the wine ages in large old oak casks (foudres) for 12 to 18 months and is bottled unfiltered ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/clos-des-papes-chateauneuf-du-pape-wine); [Skurnik](https://www.skurnik.com/producer/clos-des-papes-2/)). The usual red blend is about 65% Grenache, 20% [Mourvèdre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourv%C3%A8dre), 10% [Syrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrah) and 5% of the other permitted varieties, such as [Muscardin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscardin), [Vaccarèse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brun_Argent%C3%A9) and [Counoise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counoise). The Avrils always want a large share of Mourvèdre for its spice and backbone. About 7,000 cases are made each year.

**The vintage.** [Jancis Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jancis_Robinson)'s [vintage chart](https://www.jancisrobinson.com/learn/vintages/southern-rhone) rates 2011 in the southern Rhône as reasonably good with good yields, but not as brilliant as 2009 and 2010, with often drying tannins; with age, she says, even the best names seem a little under par. Jeb Dunnuck agreed it was "certainly a more difficult vintage", but wrote that Clos des Papes "excelled", with a rare depth of concentration. Yields were smaller than normal, just 18 hectolitres per hectare, and Paul-Vincent Avril called it a "normal blend" for the estate ([JJ Buckley, critics' notes](https://www.jjbuckley.com/wine/2011-clos-des-papes-chateauneuf-du-pape/2011-1740-750/)).

**What the critics say for 2011.** As listed by [JJ Buckley](https://www.jjbuckley.com/wine/2011-clos-des-papes-chateauneuf-du-pape/2011-1740-750/):
- **[Jeb Dunnuck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeb_Dunnuck): 92 to 95** (from foudre, September 2012). Solid intensity, medium to full body and a rich, concentrated mid-palate. Not likely to compete with 2006, 2007 or 2010, but "a mid 90-point wine that will delight Clos des Papes lovers".
- **[Wine Spectator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wine_Spectator): 95** (James Molesworth, November 2013). Pure, velvety [cassis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackcurrant) with blackberry, blood orange, singed apple wood and [bergamot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergamot_orange); succulent, with mouthwatering acidity and impressive depth for the vintage. Best 2015 to 2030; 9,000 cases.
- **Jeff Leve, [The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/clos-des-papes-chateauneuf-du-pape-wine): 94** (August 2014). Five-spice, [kirsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirsch) and pepper; soft and round, with cherry, fennel, black raspberry and a hint of spearmint.
- **[Wine Advocate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wine_Advocate): 93** (Joe Czerwinski, May 2022). Drinking well: leather, pressed flowers and black cherries; full-bodied and silky, with a complex truffle, mushroom and tree-bark note from the Mourvèdre. Drink now and over the next decade.
- **[Vinous](https://vinous.com): 93** (February 2014). Smoky cherry, red berry and potpourri; intense black raspberry and bitter cherry with a floral touch, and fine-grained tannins. Avril thought it would age well because of its balance.
- **[CellarTracker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CellarTracker) community: 93.0** (from your CellarTracker list).

**How it's drinking now.** In October 2026 the wine is fifteen years old. Your CellarTracker list gives a window of 2016 to 2030, Wine Spectator's runs to 2030, and the Wine Advocate (in 2022) gave it about a decade. So it is in its mature phase now: leather, truffle, dried flowers and soft red fruit. Drink it over the next few years rather than holding it longer. Decant gently, just to leave the sediment behind.

**Serving.** The Wine Cellar Insider suggests about 15.5°C, almost cellar temperature, for freshness and lift. Young vintages benefit from 1 to 2 hours in a [decanter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decantation); older ones need only enough to leave the sediment behind ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/clos-des-papes-chateauneuf-du-pape-wine)). The wine is unfiltered, so expect a deposit.

**Food.** The Wine Cellar Insider suggests classic meat dishes (veal, pork, beef, lamb, duck, game, roast chicken, braises, sausages and [cassoulet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassoulet)), plus mushrooms, eggplant, tomatoes and cheese. My picks: a [rack of lamb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rack_of_lamb) with garlic and herbs, a Provençal beef [daube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daube), roast duck, or a mushroom dish with a little black [truffle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuber_melanosporum). I'd avoid delicate white fish and very spicy food.

**Value and where to buy.** In the latest store lists on this site, BC Liquor carries the current 2022 at $145.99 (and the white 2022 at $135.99). Older vintages like this one now turn up mainly at auction and with fine-wine merchants such as [JJ Buckley](https://www.jjbuckley.com/). For a wine that critics rank among the very best in the appellation, I think it remains good value.

**From the history books**
- **The popes' vineyard.** In 1309 [Pope Clement V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_V) moved the papacy from Rome to [Avignon](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Palais+des+Papes,+Avignon,+France&t=k), beginning the [Avignon Papacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon_Papacy). His successor [John XXII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_XXII) improved the vineyards north of the city and built the summer [castle](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Ch%C3%A2teau+des+Papes,+Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k) that gave the village its name, "the Pope's new castle" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)). Clos des Papes takes its name from that papal past.
- **Bottled at home, 1896.** At the end of the 19th century, most Châteauneuf was sold in bulk, much of it to strengthen thinner [Burgundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgundy_wine) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)). The first Paul Avril's decision to bottle and label his own wine in 1896 made the estate one of the pioneers of estate bottling in the Rhône ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/clos-des-papes-chateauneuf-du-pape-wine)).
- **France's first appellation.** Fraud was so common in the early 20th century that the local growers, led by Baron [Pierre Le Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Le_Roy_de_Boiseaumari%C3%A9) of [Château Fortia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_Fortia), drew up rules in 1923 that became France's first [appellation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appellation_d'origine_contr%C3%B4l%C3%A9e) rules, written into law in 1936 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)). Paul Avril was one of the key people behind it ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/clos-des-papes-chateauneuf-du-pape-wine)).
- **A white since 1955.** The estate first made a white Châteauneuf in 1955, from equal parts of five varieties including [Roussanne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roussanne), [Clairette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clairette_blanche), [Bourboulenc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourboulenc) and [Picpoul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piquepoul) ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/clos-des-papes-chateauneuf-du-pape-wine)).

**Curious details**
- **The embossed bottle.** The heavy bottle with the raised papal crest is relatively new: Paul-Vincent Avril introduced it in 2002 ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/clos-des-papes-chateauneuf-du-pape-wine)).
- **A wine that lasts 80 years.** Jeff Leve of The Wine Cellar Insider wrote that a 1945 Clos des Papes was the greatest fully mature southern Rhône wine he had ever tasted.
- **"Too much Clos des Papes".** Jeb Dunnuck has written that it's almost impossible to have too much Clos des Papes in the cellar ([JJ Buckley, 2009](https://www.jjbuckley.com/wine/2009-clos-des-papes-chateauneuf-du-pape/2009-1740-750/)).
- **Tea in the glass.** Wine Spectator's James Molesworth often finds [Lapsang souchong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapsang_souchong), the smoked Chinese tea, in Clos des Papes, in both the 2009 and the 2015.
- **Mourvèdre for spine.** Clos des Papes usually puts about 20% Mourvèdre in its red, while the grape covered only about 7% of Châteauneuf's vineyards in 2004 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
